summary_text:
- Coronary artery calcium (CAC) is associated with future risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), independent of conventional risk factors [pmc_PMC5383538||ABSTRACT||000].
- CAC also improves risk prediction when added to a global risk prediction model such as the Framingham risk score [pmc_PMC5383538||ABSTRACT||000].
- The review notes that similar CAC levels across regions and ethnic groups may correspond to significantly different absolute ASCVD risk, and that no clinical trial has shown that CAC screening improves clinical outcomes or healthcare costs [pmc_PMC5383538||ABSTRACT||000].

summary_text:
- In symptomatic women and men referred for cardiac CT, coronary artery calcification (measured by coronary artery calcium score, CACS) was evaluated as a prognostic marker, and higher calcification measures were used to predict mortality. [pmc_PMC9806039||ABSTRACT||000]
- Over a median follow-up of 4.4 years, 116 patients died; the study found that MESA percentiles did not perform better than absolute CACS for predicting all-cause mortality in either women or men. [pmc_PMC9806039||ABSTRACT||000]
- Thus, coronary artery calcifications were associated with mortality risk, but sex-specific/age-specific/race-specific percentile measures did not improve prediction beyond absolute calcium score. [pmc_PMC9806039||ABSTRACT||000]

- The provided evidence does not mention coronary artery calcifications or their association with complications; it only discusses coronary blood flow abnormalities in different forms of heart failure. [pmc_PMC8758654||ABSTRACT||000]
- In ischemic heart failure, reduced coronary blood flow is described as causal to cardiac contractile dysfunction and related complications such as stunned and hibernating myocardium, coronary microembolization, myocardial infarction, and post-infarct remodeling. [pmc_PMC8758654||ABSTRACT||000]
- In non-ischemic heart failure, alterations in coronary blood flow are said to result from and contribute to cardiac contractile dysfunction, while in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction the causal contribution of coronary microvascular dysfunction is unclear. [pmc_PMC8758654||ABSTRACT||000]
